and they wept and pleaded that stones might not be hurled at them.
Now Ibn Tahir, because he was merciful,
commanded that they should not cast stones into the midst of the city,
but should strike only the wall.
Then Nasr opened the gate of the city,
and sent his three sons,
and two hundred loads of fine flour,
and three hundred loads of barley,
and five hundred sheep,
and ten horses,
and ten slaves,
and three handmaids,
and three eunuchs;
and he said:
"Tomorrow I also will come."
Then Ibn Tahir commanded the youths, saying:
"Go in to your folk,
lest they be anxious."
And at daybreak Nasr came out,
and from afar he dismounted,
and he approached, bowed down, and kissed the foot and hand of Ibn Tahir.
Then Ibn Tahir also dismounted,
and both of them sat down and conversed together secretly.
Then Ibn Tahir gave orders to Nasr, and he arose and went into the city,
on the understanding that after twenty days he would go to him at Callinicus.
And Ibn Tahir believed him in his simplicity.
And when he had taken with him Mansur, the son of Nasr himself,
he set out for Samosata,
and captured the rebel who was there.
And Nasr began to build and fortify Kaysum.
And he sent word to Ibn Tahir:
"I am prepared for war with you.
And as for Mansur my son,
do not merely imprison him in Baghdad,
but roast him in the fire and eat him!"
Then in the month of Ab, Ibn Tahir again marched against Kaysum,
and waged a fierce battle against it.
And Nasr would not allow anyone to weep over the dead.
And when the fighting grew fierce and the outer wall was breached,
Nasr again made the Christian women go up on the wall, carrying their infants and weeping.
And Ibn Tahir took pity on them,
and stopped the battle.
And the forces built houses for the winter and settled down.
And when famine grew severe in the city, so that the head of a donkey was sold for ten zuzes,
Nasr was hard pressed,
and he went out unconditionally to Ibn Tahir.
And he and his companions were conducted to Baghdad, riding upon mules.
And this deliverance from the rebels occurred in the month of Adar,
in the year one thousand one hundred and thirty-six [of the Greeks],
(825 of our Lord?).
